caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 24 of 1991.
lawyer:
Mr. A. K. M. Asaduzzaman, Advocate ------ For the defendant-appellant. 
Mr. Nazrul Islam, Advocate ------------ For the plaintiff-respondent. 
Mr. Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, AAG ------- Amicus Curiae.
parties:
James D. Sarker Prop. M/s. James Repairing  ------- Appellant
Vs.
Rajshahi Krishi Unnayan Bank  ------- Respondent
full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J.: This First Miscellaneous Appeal at the instance of the defendant- appellant is directed against an order dated 26.1.91 passed by Mr. Md. Abdus Samad, Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Rajshahi in Mortgage Suit No. 259 of 1991 allowing an application of the plaintiff under Order 38 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure for attachment of properties before Judgment. 

 3. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Artha Rin Adalat, the defendant-appellant preferred the present First Misc. Appeal in this Court. It was admitted for hearing under Order 41 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 20.2.91 by a Division Bench of this Court but the records of the Court below were not called for and the preparation of the paper book in the appeal was dispensed with. We heard this Misc. Appeal and fixed it for judgment on 6.7.92. But on that date it struck us as to whether the appeal is competent in law, the impugned order being passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. Then we again fixed this appeal for further hearing and also invited verbally Mr. Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, the learned Assistant Attorney-General to address us on the point of the maintainability of the appeal as nobody appeared for the respondent. The appeal has accordingly been further heard. At the time of further hearing, the learned Advocate Mr. Nazrul Islam appeared for the plaintiff-respondent. He then raised a preliminary objection as to the maintainability of the appeal. He has submitted that in view of the proviso of section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990 (Act 4 of 1990) which came into force on 20.1.90 hereinafter called the Act; no appeal lies against any interlocutory order (অন্তবর্তী আদেশ) passed by the Artha Rin Adalat and according to section 7 of the Act, an appeal lies only against a judgment or decree of the said Court and the period of limitation for filing such appeal in the High Court Division is 30 days and further there is also a precondition in sub-section 2 of section 7 of the Act for acceptance of the appeal that means 1/2 of the decreetal amount must be deposited by the appellant in the Court passing the decree. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the impugned order being an interlocutory order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, the present appeal against that order is wholly incompetent in law, in view of the proviso of section 7 of the Act as stated above. 

 4. Mr. Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, the learned Assistant Attorney-General while assisting this court, has taken us through the entire provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990 and then he has submitted that this Act is not a creation of the Civil Courts Act, 1887. It is a creation of and by a special Statute for some special purposes i.e. for realization of unpaid loan monies advanced by some economic establishments as defined in section 2 of the said Act. So, it is a special law as distinguishable from the general law. In sub-sections 2 and 3 of section 4 of the said Act, there are provisions for appointment of judges for the Artha Rin Adalat, by the Government in consultation with the Supreme Court. In sub-sections 4 and 5 of section 5 of the said Act there are provisions for the extent of application of the Code of Civil Procedure to the Artha Rin Adalat and its powers and procedures. In sub-section 5(Ka) subsequently introduced by an amendment vide Artha Rin Adalat Amendment Act, 1990 published on 31st July, 1990, there is a provision for limit of the adjournment of the suits and time for conclusion of the trial i.e. within six months. Then in section 6 of the said Act, there is a finality clause and bar against questioning any proceedings, order, judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat subject to section 7 of the Act regarding appeal against judgment or decree of the Artha Rin Adalat Referring to the above provisions of the Act particularly to the proviso of section 7 of the Act, the learned Assistant Attorney-General while agreeing with the submissions of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent submits that the present Misc. Appeal is wholly incompetent and not at all maintainable. 

 6. Let us now examine the relevant provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990 and consider the submissions made at the Bar and see whether the instant appeal is at all maintainable. But before examining the provisions of the Act and determining the question of maintainability of the appeal, we should keep in mind that an appeal is a creature of statute and unless a right of appeal is clearly and expressly given by the statute, it does not exist and there is no scope for inferring such a right by implication. In this regard we may look into a decision in the case of Hori Mia Vs. The State, reported in 10 DLR at page 123, which has been relied on and some other decisions reported in 3 QBD 1 page 1 and ILR 40 Calcutta at page 21 (PC). It has been observed in the above decision as follows: 

 Similar view has been expressed in the case of Jyotish Chandra Chakravarty Vs. Hem Chandra Roy and another reported in 11 DLR 7 and it is to the following effect, 

 We find similar view also expressed in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Muhammad Shari and ors. reported in PW 1979 SC (AJ & K) 117 and it is to the effect that there does not exist right of an appeal in every matter which comes for consideration of the civil Court unless such right of appeal is given by the statute or the rules made there under, inasmuch as the right of appeal is a creation of statute. Now, keeping in view the above well-settled decisions and principles regarding right of appeal, we have to examine the question of maintainability of the present appeal in the light of the provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Act. 1990. We find in the said Act that there is provision for appeal only in section 7 of the Act with certain conditions against only the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat and against no interlocutory order (অন্তবর্তী আদেশ) of the same. So far, an interlocutory order is concerned, there is an express bar against preferring any appeal as laid down in the said proviso of section 7 of the said Act. Section 7 of the said Act with its proviso runs as follows: 

 Section 6 of the Act has categorically stated that except by way of section 7 of the Act no proceedings, order, judgment or decree of the Artha Rin Adalat can be challenged or questioned before any court or authority. Thus in consideration of the above provisions of the Act and from the proviso of section 7 of the said Act, we cannot but hold that the right to appeal as provided in Order 43 r. 1 (q) against an order under rules 2, 3 and 6 of Order 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been taken away by the special provision of the proviso of section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990. As the impugned order has been passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, there is no provision for any appeal against such interlocutory order provided in the Act, rather by the proviso to section 7 of the Act a bar against appeal has been expressly created. In that view of the matter the present appeal is absolutely incompetent and is liable to be dismissed being barred by law. We are afraid whether in view of section of 6 of the Act the impugned order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat can be questioned or challenged in any court or authority. The law may appear to be harsh for taking away the right of appeal or any action against an interlocutory order of the Artha Rin Adalat, but it has to be interpreted by the Court according to the settled principles of law and the rules of interpretation, that is, while interpretating any statute its provisions should be considered as a whole bearing in mind its objects and purposes according to the principles as has been laid down in the case of AKM Ruhul Amin Vs. District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal Bhola and others, reported in 38 DLR (AD) 172 wherein, it has been observed by their Lordships as follows: 

 "In Colquhoun Vs. Brooks (1889) 14 App. case 493 (496) Lord Herschell said: It is beyond dispute, too, that we are entitled and indeed bound, when construing the terms of any provision found in statute, to consider any other parts of the Act which throw light on the intention of the legislature, and which may serve to show that the particular provision ought not to be construed as it would be alone and apart from the rest of the Act. "And Lord Davey in Canada Sugar Refining Co. Vs. R (1898) AC 735(741) said: 

 Further we have to render justice according to law as has been laid down in the case of Nur Muhammad & ors. Vs. Moulvi Mainuddin Ahmed and others reported in 39 DLR (AD) 1 to the following effect: 

 Thus, having regard to our above discussion on the point of maintainability involved in present Misc. Appeal and the principles enunciated In different cases as cited above regarding right of appeals and the rules of interpretation of statutes vis-a-vis the relevant provisions of the Act in question, we are of the view that the preliminary objection succeeds and this First Misc. Appeal must fail it being wholly incompetent in law. 

 7. In the result, this First Miscellaneous Appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
